UCI Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention Analysis

hbmaclean

2025-09-02

1 Introduction

I chose this dataset having worked in eCommerce. Below is a description of the data from UCI:

The dataset consists of feature vectors belonging to 12,330 sessions. The dataset was formed so that each session would belong to a different user in a 1-year period to avoid any tendency to a specific campaign, special day, user profile, or period.

The dataset consists of 10 numerical and 8 categorical attributes. The ‘Revenue’ attribute can be used as the class label.

“Administrative”, “Administrative Duration”, “Informational”, “Informational Duration”, “Product Related” and “Product Related Duration” represent the number of different types of pages visited by the visitor in that session and total time spent in each of these page categories. The values of these features are derived from the URL information of the pages visited by the user and updated in real time when a user takes an action, e.g. moving from one page to another.

The “Bounce Rate”, “Exit Rate” and “Page Value” features represent the metrics measured by “Google Analytics” for each page in the e-commerce site. The value of “Bounce Rate” feature for a web page refers to the percentage of visitors who enter the site from that page and then leave (“bounce”) without triggering any other requests to the analytics server during that session. The value of “Exit Rate” feature for a specific web page is calculated as for all pageviews to the page, the percentage that were the last in the session. The “Page Value” feature represents the average value for a web page that a user visited before completing an e-commerce transaction.

The “Special Day” feature indicates the closeness of the site visiting time to a specific special day (e.g. Mother’s Day, Valentine’s Day) in which the sessions are more likely to be finalized with transaction. The value of this attribute is determined by considering the dynamics of e-commerce such as the duration between the order date and delivery date. For example, for Valentina’s day, this value takes a nonzero value between February 2 and February 12, zero before and after this date unless it is close to another special day, and its maximum value of 1 on February 8.

The dataset also includes operating system, browser, region, traffic type, visitor type as returning or new visitor, a Boolean value indicating whether the date of the visit is weekend, and month of the year.

library(data.frame.X)

3 Data Creation

This downloads the zip, extracts the data file, reads and parses the lines into a data.frame and adds column names.

# Download online+shoppers+purchasing+intention+dataset.zip from UCI.edu
# and render it as a data.frame
fetch_data <- function(verbose = FALSE) {
    options(timeout = 120)
    tmp   <- tempfile()
    zip   <- paste0(
        'https://archive.ics.uci.edu',
        '/static/public/468/online+shoppers+purchasing+intention+dataset.zip'
    )
    download.file(zip, tmp, quiet = !verbose)
    data <- read_csv(unz(tmp, 'online_shoppers_intention.csv')) 

    # Here I abbreviate some of the lengthy names as given
    colnames(data) <- c(
        'Admin', 'AdminDur', 'Info', 'InfoDur', 'Prod', 'ProdDur',
        'BounceRate', 'ExitRate', 'PageVal', 'SpecialDay', 'Month',
        'OS', 'Browser', 'Region', 'TrafficType', 'VisitorType',
        'Weekend', 'Revenue'
    )
    return(data)
}

shoppers_df <- fetch_data()
shoppers_df |>
    slice_sample(n = 10) |>
    mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 1))) |>
    datatable(
        rownames = FALSE,
        options  = list(
            dom        = 't',
            scrollX    = TRUE,
            pageLength = nrow(.data)
        )
    )

3.1 Making Numeric

Making the few non-numeric columns numeric which will simplify analysis. Month, obviously, can be converted to 1:12. The two logical columns, Weekend and Revenue, can be represented as 1:0. VisitorType can be represented by 1:3 for its three distinct values:

table(shoppers_df$VisitorType) |>
    kable(col.names = c('VisitorType', 'Frequency')) |>
    kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, position = 'left')
VisitorType Frequency
New_Visitor 1694
Other 85
Returning_Visitor 10551 
shoppers_df <- shoppers_df |>
    mutate(
        Month       = coalesce(match(Month, month.abb), match(Month,month.name)),
        VisitorType = match(VisitorType, as.vector(unique(VisitorType))),
        across(where(is.logical), ~ as.integer(.x))
    )

3.2 Partitioning

index     <- createDataPartition(y = shoppers_df$Revenue, times = 1, p = 0.5, list = FALSE)
train_df  <- shoppers_df[index,]
test_df   <- shoppers_df[-index,]

From work experience, I also suspect that durations are susceptible to “cart abandonment” - shoppers leaving a session in a forgotten browser window/tab and eventually timing out.

Coupling the information above with the bar charts below, it is clear that product pages generally get lengthier looks - but also have extreme outliers (presumed abandonment); while admin- and info pages generally get brief looks - but also have outliers.

Note that the axes are scaled for better visibility of the thin end; and that the Product Page axes have a 10-fold relationship with the other durations. It does appear that the most extreme durations are associated with zero revenue - consistent with a presumed session timeout.

)

)

4.3 Near-Zero Variance

As expected, durations and rates are variable; while other columns have relatively few distinct values. None of the columns is considered to have near-zero variance, and thus nzv and zv are not worthwhile preProcess methods here.

nzv_plot(shoppers_df)

Related to nearZeroVar, checkConditonalX reports any predictor that is sparse conditioned on the levels of the outcome. Here, there is no such predictor, and thus conditionalX is not a worthwhile preProcess method here.

checkConditionalX(shoppers_df |> select(-c(Revenue)), shoppers_df$Revenue)
## integer(0)

4.4 Correlation

Two pairs, ExitRate and BounceRate, and Prod and ProdDur, have about 90% correlation. (Note that correlation is rounded to one digit for legibility.) Perhaps one from each pair can be omitted.

Browser, OS, Region, and Weekend, and TrafficType to a lesser extent, have noticeably weak correlations and sparse representation due to high p-values. Perhaps one or more can be omitted.

It is also notable that PageVal has the largest correlation with Revenue.

corr_plot(shoppers_df, tl.srt = 90, digits = 1)

4.5 Principal Component Analysis

The fact that these plots are difficult to read indicates that the variance is spread widely and fairly evenly. pca does not look like a worthwhile preProcess method here.

pca_plot(shoppers_df, pct = .90)

But oh my! Later I learned that scale is disastrous here - causes ranger to always pick the negative class; and awhile after learning that, I realized that my pca_plot had scale = TRUE for prcomp. I’ve updated that to be optional, and… one PC expains 99% of the overall variance!

pca_plot(shoppers_df, scale = FALSE, pct = .99)

Knowing that, I refer back to my coursework and its Dimension Reduction section, and plot the distance matrix for the data (a subset of it, for performance reasons) versus the prcomp rotated data of the first PC.

x        <- as.matrix(shoppers_df |> slice_sample(prop = .20))
pca      <- prcomp(x)
d        <- dist(x)
d_approx <- dist(pca$x[, 1])
plot(d, d_approx)
abline(0, 1, col = 'red')

4.6 Quick Accuracy Check

Below is a method to check accuracy via ranger.

vanilla_classification <- function(.train = train_df, .test = test_df, ...) {
    fit  <- ranger(factor(Revenue) ~ ., .train, ...)
    pred <- predict(fit, .test)
    cols <- c('Prevalence', 'Sensitivity', 'Specificity', 'Precision', 'F1')
    .cm  <- confusionMatrix(pred$predictions, factor(.test$Revenue))
    .cm$byClass |>
        as.data.frame() |>
        rownames_to_column(var = 'Class') |>
        tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = c(1), values_from = c(2)) |>
        select(all_of(cols)) |>
        mutate(
            Accuracy = .cm$overall[['Accuracy']],
            across(everything(), ~ sprintf('%.2f', .x * 100))
        ) |>
        kable(
            digits  = 3,
            caption = 'Ranger Classification Metrics'
        ) |>
        kable_styling(
            bootstrap_options = 'bordered',
            full_width = FALSE,
            position = 'left'
        )
}
vanilla_classification()
Ranger Classification Metrics
Prevalence Sensitivity Specificity Precision F1 Accuracy
84.23 96.17 58.44 92.52 94.31 90.22

90% seems good - but is only 5% better than simply guessing the negative outcome.

4.7 Positive Class

By default, TRUE/FALSE and 1/0 are factored into the reverse order; but in this case, logically, Revenue=TRUE is positive. Does the order have any bearing?

vanilla_classification(
    .train = train_df |> mutate(Revenue = reorder(factor(Revenue), Revenue, decreasing=TRUE)),
    .test  = test_df  |> mutate(Revenue = reorder(factor(Revenue), Revenue, decreasing=TRUE))
)
Ranger Classification Metrics
Prevalence Sensitivity Specificity Precision F1 Accuracy
15.77 57.92 96.19 73.98 64.97 90.15

I think this is clarifying, so I will lock in that change.

  • Prevalence now reflects the positive class
  • Sensitivity and Specificity are in keeping with their definitions - True Positive and True Negative
  • F1 is much lower because it is based upon Sensitivity and Precision
  • Accuracy is essentially unchanged
train_df <- train_df |>
    mutate(Revenue = reorder(factor(Revenue), Revenue, decreasing=TRUE))
test_df  <- test_df |>
    mutate(Revenue = reorder(factor(Revenue), Revenue, decreasing=TRUE))

4.8 Omitting Columns

Noted above in Correlation, OS, Browser, Region, Weekend, and TrafficType have relatively few and weak correlations; while ExitRate correlates strongly with BounceRate. I omitted numerous combinations and find that these six can be dropped without ill-effect - even perhaps a slight improvement, especially for Specificity.

train_df <- train_df |> select(-c(OS,Browser,Region,Weekend,TrafficType,ExitRate))
test_df  <- test_df  |> select(-c(OS,Browser,Region,Weekend,TrafficType,ExitRate))

vanilla_classification()

Prevalence Sensitivity Specificity Precision F1 Accuracy

Noted above in Missing, Duplicate, and Outlying Values, there are 125 duplicate rows. I have learned to be cautious about removing them - and here again it reduces accuracy.

4.10 Class Weights

For earlier projects, I’ve referred to this article for weighing classes to overcome an imbalance. This does seem to help. Numbers change with every run, but Sensitivity is generally improved - which is precisely the goal, to more accurately predict true positives despite the low prevalence.

class_weights <- c(
    nrow(train_df) / (2 * sum(train_df$Revenue==1)),
    nrow(train_df) / (2 * sum(train_df$Revenue==0))
)
vanilla_classification(class.weights = class_weights)
Ranger Classification Metrics
Prevalence Sensitivity Specificity Precision F1 Accuracy
15.77 61.11 95.13 70.13 65.31 89.76

4.11 Case Weights

There are also case.weights, for weighing the observations. I made two educated guesses as to weighing the rows. The first method is ineffective; the second method may be very slightly effective - in reference to the results from switching the Positive Class.

  1. Sum across rows the values of three booleans - whether the Prod/Admin/Info page durations are outliers; then exaggerate the results from 0:3 to 1:20 with exp; and finally inverse the results, such that having no outlier equals 1 and having three outliers equals 1/20.

    case_weights <- 1 / exp(
    rowSums(
        rstatix::is_outlier(
            train_df |>
                select(c(ProdDur, AdminDur, InfoDur)) |>
                as.matrix())
))
vanilla_classification(case.weights = case_weights)

  2. Use ntile to spread the cumulative page durations into 50 buckets.

    mutate(DurationBucket = ntile(ProdDur+AdminDur+InfoDur, 50)) |> pull(DurationBucket)

4.12 Impute Outliers

Here I impute outliers with median values. It proves to be ineffective; and factors are a mixed blessing…

train_o      <- train_df |> mutate(Revenue = varhandle::unfactor(Revenue)) |> as.matrix()
outliers     <- rstatix::is_outlier(train_o[,c('ProdDur', 'InfoDur', 'AdminDur')])
idx          <- which(outliers)
train_o[idx] <- NA
train_o      <- train_o |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    mutate(Revenue = reorder(factor(Revenue), Revenue, decreasing=TRUE))

test_o       <- test_df |> mutate(Revenue = varhandle::unfactor(Revenue)) |> as.matrix()
outliers     <- rstatix::is_outlier(test_o[,c('ProdDur', 'InfoDur', 'AdminDur')])
idx          <- which(outliers)
test_o[idx]  <- NA
test_o       <- test_o |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    mutate(Revenue = reorder(factor(Revenue), Revenue, decreasing=TRUE))

vanilla_classification(
    .train = impute_median(train_o),
    .test  = impute_median(test_o)
)
Ranger Classification Metrics
Prevalence Sensitivity Specificity Precision F1 Accuracy
15.77 60.29 95.44 71.20 65.29 89.89

4.13 Scale and Center

Heh, it seems scaling/centering causes ranger to always predict the negative class. The same is true when just centering (scale = FALSE) and just scaling (center = FALSE).

vanilla_classification(
    .train = train_df |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ scale(.x)[1])),
    .test  = test_df  |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ scale(.x)[1]))
)
Ranger Classification Metrics
Prevalence Sensitivity Specificity Precision F1 Accuracy
15.77 0.00 100.00 NA NA 84.23

4.14 Initial Conclusions

Omitting columns with weak correlations and high p-values was NOT harmful, and thus considered worthwhile.

Switching the positive class by reversing the natural factor order of Revenue shifts and clarifies the metrics, particularly Prevalence, Specificity and Sensitivity - without affecting accuracy.

Case weights are somewhat effective for balancing the two outcomes.

Omitting duplicates, imputing outliers, and scaling and centering are non-starters.

Looking ahead to train and the flexibility it provides, and probably another model or few, I have already ruled out numerous preProcess options:

  • corr (correlation)
  • nzv, zv, and conditionalX (variance-related)
  • scale, center
  • median_impute (NA’d outliers)

5 Additional Models

Here I try some other classification models for comparison.

First, a configuration - for each model, a simple function/wrapper of the model and the required type for predict.

model_config <- list(
    ranger       = list(
        FUNC = function(...) { ranger(...) },
        TYPE = 'response'
    ),
    randomForest = list(
        FUNC = function(...) { randomForest(...) },
        TYPE = 'response'
    ),
    knn3         = list(
        FUNC = function(...) { knn3(...) },
        TYPE = 'class'
    ),
    naive_bayes  = list(
        FUNC = function(...) { naive_bayes(...) },
        TYPE = 'class'
    ),
    multinom     = list(
        FUNC = function(...) { multinom(...) },
        TYPE = 'class'
    )
)

And methods for predictions, wrapping predict with some intelligence and error checking; and for accuracy, wrapping the call to predict and confusionMatrix with error checking.

predictions <- function(model, test_df, type = 'class') {
    tryCatch({
        .pred <- predict(model, test_df, type = type)
    }, 
    error = function(e) {
        print(c(Model = model, error = e))
    },
    finally = {
        if(!is.atomic(.pred)) {
            .pred <- .pred$predictions
        }
        return(.pred)
    })
}

accuracy <- function(model, test_df, ...) {
    tryCatch({
        .pred <- predictions(model, test_df, ...)
        .cm   <- confusionMatrix(.pred, as.factor(test_df$Revenue))
    },
    error = function(e) {
        print(c(Model = model, error = e))
    },
    finally = {
        if (!exists('.cm')) {
            return(NA)
        }
        else {
            return(round(100*.cm$overall[['Accuracy']],2))
        }
    })
}

And a “private” function to run a single model, with a caller to run all models in the configuration.

fc <- as.formula(factor(Revenue) ~ .)
.run_model <- function(cfg, .formula, .train, .test) {
    FUNC <- cfg$FUNC
    TYPE <- cfg$TYPE
    accuracy(
        get("FUNC")(.formula, .train),
        .test, type = TYPE
    )
}

run_models <- function(
        .models  = model_config,
        .formula = fc,
        .train   = train_df,
        .test    = test_df
    ) {
        results <- sapply(names(.models), function(model) {
            .run_model(.models[[model]], .formula, .train, .test)
        })
        names(results) <- names(.models)
        return(results)
}

Finally I run the models. It seems ranger was a fine first pick; with randomForest keeping it company at about 90%.

shush <- capture.output({
    baselines <- run_models()
})
baselines |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    arrange(desc(baselines)) |>
    kable(col.names = c('Model', 'Accuracy')) |>
    kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, position = 'left')
Model Accuracy
randomForest 89.89
ranger 89.75
multinom 88.08
knn3 85.99
naive_bayes 82.71

6 Training Several Models

Now I look to train and the flexibility it provides. Similar to earlier, here is a “private” function to run a single model, and a caller to run all models in the configuration.

.train_model  <- function(
        model, cfg, .formula, .train, .test, bestTune,
       .trControl = NULL, .preProcess = NULL
) {
    tryCatch({
        fit <- (function(...) {
            caret::train(
                .formula,
                method     = model,
                data       = .train,
                trControl  = dplyr::coalesce(
                    .trControl,
                    trainControl(
                        method = 'repeatedcv',
                        number = 2,
                        p      = .5
                    )
                ),
                tuneGrid   = cfg$tuneGrid,
                preProcess = .preProcess,
                ...
            )
        })() # ideally, (...) 
    }, error = function(e) {
        print(c(Model = model, error = e))
    },
    finally = {
        if (exists('fit')) {
            .acc <- accuracy(fit, .test, type = dplyr::coalesce(cfg$type, 'raw'))

            if (bestTune) {
                return(
                    c(
                        Model    = model,
                        Accuracy = .acc,
                        bestTune = paste(
                            sapply(1:length(fit$bestTune), function(i) {
                                paste(
                                    names(fit$bestTune)[i],
                                    fit$bestTune[[i]],
                                    sep = '='
                                )
                            }),
                            collapse = ', '
                        )
                    )
                )
            }
            else {
                return(.acc)
            }
        }
    })
}

train_models <- function(
    .config       = train_config,
    .formula      = fc,
    .train        = train_df,
    .test         = test_df,
    bestTune      = FALSE,
    .trControl    = NULL,
    .preProcess   = NULL
) {
    results <- sapply(names(.config), function(model) {
        .train_model(
            model, .config[[model]], .formula, .train, .test,
            bestTune, .trControl, .preProcess
        )
    })
    names(results) <- names(.config)
    return(results)
}

6.1 tuneGrid

And here, another configuration structure, with model-specific tuneGrid objects - initially NULL for a baseline reference.

Now another run with tuneGrid parameters spanning the initial best values. Having used xgbTree before, I know to be careful with its sprawling tuneGrid - to not create too many permutations.

train_config <- list(
    ranger = list(
        tuneGrid = expand.grid(
            mtry          = c(2,4,6,8),
            splitrule     = c('gini', 'extratrees'),
            min.node.size = c(1,5,10,20)
        )
    ),
    rf = list(
        tuneGrid = expand.grid(
            mtry = c(2,4,6,8)
        )
    ),
    Rborist = list(
        tuneGrid = expand.grid(
            predFixed = c(2,4,6,8),
            minNode   = c(1,2,5,10)
        )
    ),
    treebag = list(
        tuneGrid = NULL
    ),
    xgbTree = list(
        tuneGrid = expand.grid(
            nrounds          = 50,
            max_depth        = c(2,4,10),
            eta              = c(0.01, 0.1, 0.4),
            gamma            = c(0, .3),
            colsample_bytree = 0.6,
            min_child_weight = c(1,3,5),
            subsample        = 1
        )
    ),
    svmRadial = list(
        tuneGrid = expand.grid(
            sigma = c(.001, .01, .1, .3),
            C     = c(.5, 1, 5, 10)
        )
    )
)

Well, I have never really had much luck making improvements via tuneGrid. I suspect models already do the same - try ranges of values and hone in on the best. Some values did change, but accuracy was never improved significantly. Fruitless again, other than maybe xgbTree, and figuring out a solution for presenting bestTune values.

shush <- capture.output({
    bestTunesII <- train_models(bestTune = TRUE)
})

t(unname(bestTunesII)) |>
    kable(col.names = c('Model', 'Accuracy', 'bestTune')) |>
    kable_styling(
        full_width = FALSE,
        position   = 'left',
        bootstrap_options = c('bordered', 'striped')
    )

6.2 preProcess

I have already ruled out many preProcess options in my initial conclusions. Here I try BoxCox, YeoJohnson, spacialSign and pca. I tried expoTrans as well, but it spewed Expo. transform induced infinite values in several predictors and is ommitted: AdminDur, InfoDur, ProdDur.

display_summary <- function(.data) {
    .data |>
        dplyr::rename(` ` = c(1)) |>
        datatable(
            rownames = FALSE,
            options  = list(
                dom        = 't',
                pageLength = nrow(.data)
            )
        )
}
shush <- capture.output({
    pre_results <- bind_rows(
        train_models(.preProcess = 'BoxCox'),
        train_models(.preProcess = 'YeoJohnson'),
        train_models(.preProcess = 'spatialSign'),
        train_models(.preProcess = 'pca',
            .trControl = trainControl(
                preProcOptions = list(thresh = .99),
                method = 'repeatedcv',
                number = 2,
                p      = .5
            )
        )
    )
})

pre_summary <- bind_cols(
    c('BoxCox', 'YeoJohnson', 'spatialSign', 'pca'),
    pre_results
)

display_summary(pre_summary)

6.3 trainControl

boot_results <- bind_rows(
    train_models(.trControl = trainControl(
        method = 'boot', number = 2)),
    train_models(.trControl = trainControl(
        method = 'boot632', number = 2)),
    train_models(.trControl = trainControl(
        method = 'optimism_boot', number = 2)),
    train_models(.trControl = trainControl(
        method = 'boot_all', number = 2))
)

cv_results <- bind_rows(
    train_models(.trControl = trainControl(
        method = 'cv', p = .5, repeats = 2, number = 2)),
    train_models(.trControl = trainControl(
        method = 'repeatedcv', p = .5, repeats = 2, number = 2)),
    train_models(.trControl = trainControl(
        method = 'LGOCV', p = .5, repeats = 2, number = 2))
)

train_summary <- bind_cols(
    c(
        'boot', 'boot632', 'optimism_boot', 'boot_all',
        'cv', 'repeatedcv', 'LGOCV'
    ),
    bind_rows(boot_results, cv_results)
)

display_summary(train_summary)

7 Focus on xgbTree

I do not know how authoritative this visual-xgboost-tuning-with-caret article is, but it seems knowledgeable. Here, I follow it quite closely, in my own style.

shush <- capture.output({
    xgb <- caret::train(
        fc,
        method     = 'xgbTree',
        data       = train_df,
        trControl  = trainControl(
                        method = 'cv',
                        number = 3
                    ),
        tuneGrid   = expand.grid(
            nrounds          = seq(200, 1000, 50),
            eta              = c(0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.3),
            max_depth        = 2:6,
            min_child_weight = 1,
            colsample_bytree = 1,
            subsample        = 1,
            gamma            = 0
        )
    )
})

Here I plot accuracy per max_depth versus nrounds, faceted by eta.

xgb$results |>
    ggplot(aes(nrounds, Accuracy, color = factor(max_depth))) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_line() +
    facet_wrap(~eta) + 
    labs(color = 'Max Tree Depth') +
    ggtitle(
        'Accuracy vs. N-Rounds per Tree Depth, Faceted by eta',
        subtitle = sprintf('Best Accuracy, %.2f', max(xgb$results$Accuracy)*100)
    )

Best accuracy above should align with bestTune:

xgb$bestTune |>
    as_tibble() |>
    kable(caption = sprintf('Accuracy %%%.2f', max(xgb$results$Accuracy)*100)) |>
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = 'bordered')
Accuracy %90.17
nrounds max_depth eta gamma colsample_bytree min_child_weight subsample
200 2 0.05 0 1 1 1

Here I lock in the “best” eta; continue flexing on max_depth; and add variability for min_child_weight.

shush <- capture.output({

            max_depth        = 2:5,
            min_child_weight = 1:4,
            colsample_bytree = 1,

            gamma            = 0

})

Here, I plot accuracy per min_child_weight versus nrounds, faceted by max_depth.

Here I lock in “best” max_depth and min_child_weight, along with eta; and create sequences for colsample_bytree and subsample. (Again, being cautious about the size of tuneGrid - here, 250 permutations.)

min_child_weight <- xgb$bestTune$min_child_weight

shush <- capture.output({

Well, that does give the best accuracy during this process - this time, but the results are ever-changing despite seed. Here I lock in the “best” gamma, and incorporate ‘YeoJohnson’ as a preProcess method, and replace ‘cv’ with ‘optimism_boot’ for the trainControl method - two items that made minor improvements for this model earlier.

gamma <- xgb$bestTune$gamma

shush <- capture.output({
    xgb <- caret::train(
        fc,
        method     = 'xgbTree',
        data       = train_df,
        trControl  = trainControl(method = 'optimism_boot'),
        tuneGrid   = expand.grid(
            nrounds          = seq(200, 1000, 50),
            eta              = eta,
            max_depth        = max_depth,
            min_child_weight = min_child_weight,
            colsample_bytree = colsample_bytree,
            subsample        = subsample,
            gamma            = gamma
        ),
        preProcess = c('YeoJohnson')
    )
})

Inspect bestTune and resulting accuracy:

xgb$bestTune |>
    as_tibble() |>
    kable(caption = sprintf('Accuracy %%%.2f', max(xgb$results$Accuracy)*100)) |>
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = 'bordered')

        fc,

        data       = train_df,
        trControl  = trainControl(
            method         = 'optimism_boot',
            preProcOptions = list(thresh = .99)

            nrounds          = nrounds,

})

8 Decision Tree

I like to finish with a glimpse at a decision tree, for a sense of the inner mechanics.

fit                   <- randomForest(Revenue ~ ., train_df, ntree = 20)
simplest_tree         <- which.min(fit$forest$ndbigtree)
fit$forest$xbestsplit <- round(fit$forest$xbestsplit, 2)  # 'digits' workaround
plot.getTree(
    fit,
    k     = simplest_tree,
    depth = 6,
    main  = sprintf(
         'RandomForest Decision Tree - Accuracy %.2f',
         accuracy(fit, test_df)
    )
)

9 Conclusions

Again, my primary goal was continued learning. I used t to rotate bestTune objects, after pondering pivot_wider and pivot_longer; discovered capture.output to silence unwanted messages; had my first opportunity since classwork to look at dist (for other projects, it ran out of memory or simply seemed inapplicable); and realized my error of assuming scale=TRUE for prcomp.

Once again though, while I am able to fairly quickly identify one good model from many, I seem unable to make measurable improvements with preProcess, trainControl, tuneGrid, imputing outliers, reducing dimensions, or other attempts.

Four models slightly exceeded 90%, but none consistently stood out.

In this case, I pause with a working model; disappointed that it is merely 5% better than guessing, and frustrated that I could not overcome the class imbalance.
